# Parse error: syntax error, unexpected end of file, expecting elseif (T_ELSEIF) or else (T_ELSE) or endif (T_ENDIF) When you encounter a PHP parse error stating `syntax error, unexpected end of file` while working with Blade templates, the compiler is screaming that it expected a closing directive but hit the end of the script instead. In your specific case, the error log explicitly mentions expecting `elseif`, `else`, or `endif`. This tells us exactly where the logic flow broke down: inside an `@if` block that was never closed with its corresponding `@endif`. Looking at the provided `customers_blade.php` view, the code structure immediately reveals the culprit. You open a conditional check for a success message using `@if(Session::has('success'))`. Following that is a nested check for a warning message: `@if(Session::has(warning))`. However, the logic never resolves. The inner block closes with `@endif`, but the outer block containing the success message remains open all the way to the end of the file. Here is the problematic segment from your code: ```blade @if(Session::has('success'))
{{Session :: get('message')}}
@if(Session::has(warning))
{{Session::get('message')}}
@endif
``` Because the parser reads to the bottom of the file without finding the matching `@endif` for the first condition, it throws the syntax error you are seeing. The solution is straightforward: add `@endif` before the `
` element that starts the file input label. Beyond fixing the immediate syntax error, there are a few architectural considerations worth addressing in your implementation of the customer import blade. First, notice the variable inconsistency between the two alerts. You use `Session::get('message')` for the warning alert but `Session :: get('message')` for the success alert. While this might work if the session key is strictly 'message' for both, it is often best practice to store distinct keys like `'success_message'` and `'warning_message'` or ensure your controller explicitly sets the same key name. Mixing these up can lead to silent failures where alerts don't render even if the code is syntactically correct. Secondly, look at how you are displaying errors.
